title: Water for the Other Side
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The spreadsheet said we had enough water.

The people waiting at the east end of the bridge said otherwise.

I stared at the figures and felt my face grow warm. The table I'd made showed thirty containers delivered to Riverstone Terrace, twelve to the clinic, eight to Brasswatch Yard, and six to the temporary shelter on the ridge. The total matched the supply account.

It was beautiful arithmetic.

It was a terrible distribution.

Katara stood beside me, reading the paper.

"How many people are at the east shelter?" she asked.

"Eighteen."

"And at the west?"

"Seven."

"How many containers?"

"Six east. Ten west."

She tapped the page.

"There's our problem."

The bridge had remained closed while the supports were repaired and tested after the storm. People could use the longer ridge route, but not every family could carry heavy containers that distance. The supply team had delivered water to the places closest to the storage depot first, then sent what remained to the harder-to-reach shelter.

Nobody had set out to be cruel.

The process had been convenient for the people carrying the crates, not fair to those who needed them.

I reached for my pencil.

"We can fix the numbers."

"Eventually," Katara said. "But first we need to talk to the people who are short."

We walked to the east shelter with Aang. The wind was still strong along the canal, and the lower path smelled of wet stone. A temporary ramp led into the hall, built after Edda's access inspection.

A woman named Sela greeted us at the door.

"Do you have water?"

"Some," Katara said. "Not enough yet. We're checking what everyone needs."

Sela pointed to a row of empty vessels.

"Some of us can drink from the spring if we carry it. Others can't carry the distance. The oldest person here needs water brought to her, and the family with the baby is boiling what they can find."

Katara nodded.

"Then they go first."

I wrote down the specific needs without putting private names on the public board.

Aang looked at the route.

"I could carry water across the canal with bending."

Sela looked at him.

"You could. What happens when you leave?"

He hesitated.

"We need a system that doesn't depend on me."

"Yes."

I felt a small rush of admiration. He'd learned to hear that question without treating it as an insult.

We returned to the square and called the distribution volunteers together. Mara had been packing supplies, Danse had helped design the carrying frames, and Greg had offered a morning shift with the handcart. Toph stood near the wall, listening to the movement through the stone floor.

I put the numbers on the board.

"These are the deliveries," I said. "But this is not the same as the needs."

One volunteer frowned.

"We delivered to every district."

"Yes. We didn't deliver proportionately to the people who couldn't access the other supplies."

Another looked embarrassed.

"We used the closest route first."

"I know. That's why we're changing it."

Toph tapped the floor.

"Your chart counts containers. It doesn't count the distance a person has to drag them."

I looked at her.

"Exactly."

We made a new plan with actual requirements. Katara confirmed the clinic's medical supply needs. Sela arranged a contact person at the east shelter without making the residents' private details public. Danse checked the handcart load. Edda tested the route so the deliveries wouldn't block the accessible path.

Aster came from Brasswatch carrying a spare lamp and a note with a corner torn away. They had been checking the backup lights near the workshop when somebody found water pooling beside the service junction.

“Renn says the generator may have to stay down tonight,” Aster told us. “We need the drinking-water cart to use the north entrance. The service corridor's being kept clear for electrical inspection.”

I looked at my chart. The fastest route to the east shelter ran past the very doorway Aster had named. A quicker path for water would now send a heavy cart through a place where someone could be working on wet cables.

“Can the shelter wait until morning?” I asked.

Amel, who had walked over with the latest request sheet, gave me a look that made my ears burn.

“No. People are drinking the last of their reserve tonight.”

Toph tapped the paving with her heel. “Then find another route. The water isn't going to sprout legs because your chart says it's inconvenient.”

Aang volunteered to carry the first two containers himself. Katara stopped him long enough to ask whether somebody could do the rest without the Avatar. Beren, who was loading the cart, drew the wider path on the back of my old delivery sheet. Edda walked it with him, checked the turns, and marked where a loose crate would narrow the entrance.

Aster folded the new route into their pocket to show Danse before the lights failed altogether.

It meant the water would arrive later, but by a path we had actually tested. I had spent so much time making the first numbers look balanced that I had almost delivered water into an electrical hazard.

When I crossed out the old line, the ink ran through two entire columns. I didn't bother making it neat. I wrote the new arrival time in the space below and asked Amel to read it back to me.

Aang offered to carry the heaviest containers for the first round, with two local volunteers learning the handling process for later shifts.

No one was assigned more than they'd agreed to do.

The revised plan meant the west shelter would receive fewer extra containers for one day. Some residents complained. They had been relieved to have a reserve and did not like hearing that it had been allocated unevenly.

I couldn't blame them for feeling anxious.

I could still tell the truth.

"We're not taking away your minimum needs," I explained. "We're correcting a distribution that left another group without theirs."

A man near the depot folded his arms.

"Easy for you to say."

He was right about one thing: I was not the person who would have to walk farther for water if the plan failed.

"Then help us test it," I said.

He looked surprised.

"We need your experience of the route. And if you find a problem, I want to know."

He did.

We took the draft to the east shelter before asking anyone to call it fair. A woman named Amel was distributing cups near the entrance. She held the sheet with two fingers, as though it might leave ink on her hands.

"Thirty containers," she read. "For the whole terrace?"

"Yes."

"How many of those are supposed to arrive before the night shift starts?"

I checked. "Twelve."

She tapped a line with her nail. "We have six people working outside until dark. They won't be here to collect water at that hour."

I was ready to explain the schedule, then stopped. The schedule was mine. The people waiting for water hadn't agreed to live according to it.

"What time would actually work?" I asked.

She wrote two possible windows in the margin, then asked whether the depot could hold a few containers for people who preferred not to explain their household arrangements in public. Katara said the shelter could record quantities without publishing names. That was different from hiding how much water it had received.

Aang wanted to help with deliveries. Amel looked at his glider.

"Not everything can arrive from the sky," she said. "Some people need to know what happens when you're not here."

He winced, then nodded. "You're right."

Toph tested the stone lip of the north path with her foot. "And the cart still has to turn a corner. Which brilliant person drew that?"

I raised my hand.

"Of course you did."

I laughed despite the heat in my cheeks. She wasn't gentle about an error, but she didn't make me afraid to change it. There was affection in her bluntness, and I wasn't required to enjoy it every minute to know she cared.

When the sheet finally had a plan that Amel could use, I passed her the pen. She signed the receipt for the proposed time, not for water that had yet to arrive.

"Come back when the carts do," she said.

We did. The plan still needed a driver's eye before it could become a real route.

The first revision nearly failed at the depot.

A cart driver named Beren looked at the new sheet and shook his head.

"You've moved the east delivery earlier, but you're still using the narrow lane by the canal. My cart can't turn around there when the rain comes."

I studied the map. He was right. In my hurry to fix the unequal water totals, I had reused the old route without checking whether the carriers could actually make the journey.

"Which path would you use?" I asked.

"The north path. Longer, but the stones are solid."

Toph tapped her foot against the ground.

"He's right about the surface."

"Can Edda check the turns?" Katara asked.

"Already did yesterday," Beren said. "I watched her. She made me move a stack of crates so she could pass."

I looked up.

"Thank you for doing that."

"She didn't ask politely."

Toph grinned. "Sounds like Edda."

We changed the route.

Aang offered to carry the heaviest containers along the first run, but Sela reminded him that the local volunteers needed practice managing the handcart without bending. They divided the loads by what people could safely handle. Aang worked with them, not instead of them.

At the east shelter, a woman asked whether the delivery record would name the people who received extra water.

"No," Katara said. "The public record will show how much arrived and what needs it served. Your medical or family details aren't for the notice board."

The woman nodded and accepted the containers.

I crossed out another line on the spreadsheet. The new table looked worse than the old one. It had arrows, corrections, and a reminder to review the distribution after two days.

It was also the first version that people who used the routes had helped write.

I had spent so long worrying about being a responsible member of our complicated household that I'd forgotten the same principle mattered outside our door. Caring for people wasn't making decisions for them. It was asking which decisions actually changed the day they had to live.

The second delivery went better. The east shelter received its immediate supplies before evening. The west retained enough for confirmed needs. The public ledger showed the changes and the reasons, without turning vulnerable households into a list of people to be judged.

We returned home exhausted.

Katara washed the dust from her hands and looked at my spreadsheet, now covered in corrections.

"Do you still like it?" she asked.

"Not particularly."

She smiled.

"Good. That means it's being used."

Toph sat at the table with a bowl of soup.

"Spreadsheets are like people," she announced. "They get annoying when they think they're always right."

Aang laughed.

I sat beside her.

"Are you comparing me to a spreadsheet?"

"Only on your worst days."

Katara came around the table and rested a hand on my shoulder.

"You noticed a problem," she said. "Then you listened. That's what matters."

I looked at her.

"We still missed it for two days."

"Yes."

She didn't soften the truth.

Then she kissed my forehead.

"We'll do better tomorrow."

Later, when the dishes were done, Aang showed me the new route he'd drawn. It included shaded rest points, safe crossing times, and notes from the people who used the path daily. His handwriting was crooked from trying to fit too much information onto one page.

I smiled.

"It looks terrible."

"It works."

"That might be the new standard."

He grinned and leaned close.

"Then perhaps I can ask for something that doesn't fit in a table."

"What?"

"A quiet walk with you."

I took his hand.

We went outside beneath the lanterns.

The bridge remained closed. The water was still moving. The arithmetic was still imperfect.

But the people on the other side had water, and we'd stopped confusing a balanced column with a fair day.
